PolSo on the STM32G474

Running parameters, computation cost and how to verify it. A virtual NUCLEO-G474RE (Cortex-M4F, 170 MHz, 128 KB SRAM, 512 KB flash) running the real firmware core, plus a rehearsed verification plan. Generated 2026-10-14.

SummaryRunning parametersComputationEnergy What to verify againstRehearsalChangesOn the board
What this is and is not. No ARM compiler, emulator or board was available. The operation counts are exact for your firmware source (the unchanged C code was built with every floating-point operation counted). The cycle costs per operation, the currents and the SD-card behaviour are estimates with low / nominal / high ranges (stm32_twin/spec.py); conclusions are stated only where they hold across the range. Benchmark firmware and a comparison tool are included so each estimate can be replaced by a measurement in the first week.

Summary

476 µsCPU time per 30 s hop, reference firmware (81 k cycles at 170 MHz)
0.038%of the time the core is running (optimised architecture)
8.0 → 0.9 mAaverage MCU current: typical starter firmware → optimised architecture
11 KB / 59 KBSRAM / flash used, of 128 / 512 KB
2.0 daysbattery life on 2000 mAh with every lever (7 h as specified)
  1. Compute is not the constraint. One 30 s hop of the whole pipeline (parsing, compensation, 25 features, int8 MLP, confidence gate) costs about 81 k cycles, 476 µs and 28 µJ at 170 MHz. That is 0.0016% of the CPU. Even with the pessimistic cost assumptions it stays below 0.003%.
  2. What decides MCU energy is the firmware architecture, not the algorithm. The same pipeline draws 8.0 mA with a typical HAL starter project (1 ms SysTick, blocking SD writes, 8-sentence GPS) and 0.90 mA with tickless Stop 1 idle, DMA-driven SD, an RMC-only GPS and register-level drivers. Optimising the computation on top of that (0.90 → 0.90 mA) changes almost nothing.
  3. The MCU is a small part of the battery budget. In the as-specified design the PMS7003 fan and laser take 53% of the battery current; the MCU in the best design is 3%. Duty-cycling the PMS7003, dropping the Nucleo board and slowing the GPS take battery life from 7 h to 48 h (2.0 days).
  4. Accuracy rises only slowly with model size, so choose the model by accuracy, not by cost. On held-out simulated field sessions macro-F1 runs from 0.90 (logistic regression, 1,825 cycles) to 0.96 (MLP int8 128-64, 44,696 cycles, 263 µs); the deployed MLP 25-32-16-5 scores 0.94. The intervals overlap, so small rankings are not supported. What is supported: every candidate uses under 0.001% of the CPU, so the compute budget never forces a trade-off with accuracy.
  5. Duty-cycling the PMS7003 is cheap in accuracy; waking it from the gas signal does not work. In a busy site a 1/3 duty cycle keeps 84% of the answers right against 86% with the fan always on; in a quiet site 1/6 duty keeps 93% against 96%. The gas-triggered policy reached only 69% in the quiet site because dust has no gas signature.
  6. PM2.5 mass does not meet the EPA targets in the rehearsal, and 12 days is too few to fit more than a humidity correction. The raw device reads 1.9x the reference (R² 0.83), because low-cost counters read different sources differently. A humidity correction, scored by cross-validation over days, brings the slope to 1.30 (R² 0.82, RMSE 73 µg/m³ over hours up to 475 µg/m³). A correction in which the device's own source label chooses the gain did worse (R² 0.67): six parameters fitted from a short, heavy-tailed record do not generalise. Plan at least 30 days of co-location and always report the cross-validated result.
  7. The verification rehearsal met 5 of 9 proposed criteria. That is a statement about the simulator and the metrics, not about the hardware, but it shows the pipeline, file formats and sample sizes work before any data exists.

What you can claim, and on what evidence

ClaimStatusEvidence and what is missing
The complete attribution pipeline runs on a Cortex-M4F in a few hundred microseconds per 30 s window using about 11 KB of SRAM and 59 KB of flashSUPPORTED IN SIMULATIONOperation counts are exact; cycle costs and memory are ranges. Confirm with bench/dwt_bench.c and the linker map.
Architecture-level co-design cuts MCU energy about 9x without changing the algorithmSUPPORTED IN SIMULATIONNeeds a current measurement across the Nucleo IDD jumper; the Stop 1 and Run currents are the sensitive inputs.
Caching the log, averaging before decimating the humidity term and using a polynomial log / exp cut compute by 41% with the same labelsSUPPORTED IN SIMULATIONLog caching is bit-identical; the others change 1 of 357 windows (an answer becoming “uncertain”) and none between two different sources.
Compute budget does not limit accuracy: even the largest candidate model needs a tiny fraction of the CPUSUPPORTED IN SIMULATIONHolds on simulated data. Which model is most accurate on real sensors is open: repeat the comparison on real data.
A source-aware PM2.5 correction improves mass accuracyNOT SUPPORTEDDid not beat the humidity-only correction with 12 days in the rehearsal, and the composition bias it targets is an assumption of the simulator. Revisit with 30+ days of real data.
The approach is novel compared with existing workNOT SUPPORTEDPrior art was not surveyed here. Check before claiming novelty; the comparison slide already names IIT Kanpur's DHSA as closest.

The window task is 117 µs every 30 s. The SD write is the only slow CPU step (353 µs of CPU) and its card-side wait, which can reach a second on a bad card, is why it must not block the main loop.

A simulated logic-analyser view

1.2 s around a 30 s window boundary. Blue: peripheral busy moving bytes (UART frames, I²C, SPI). Orange: CPU running. In A0 the SD write busy-waits with the CPU running for as long as the card takes (a few milliseconds here, hundreds on a slow write); in A4 it is DMA and the CPU sleeps.

The 30 s window task itself: feature extraction and the int8 MLP take well under a millisecond.

Simulated current at the MCU supply pin

What a power profiler would show for the same 1.2 s. The starter firmware sits at the Sleep floor and wakes every millisecond (middle panel), so it never reaches Stop 1; the optimised one spends most of its time there.

Every step is a design choice, not an algorithm change: tickless idle (the 1 ms HAL tick forbids Stop), DMA-driven SD logging (no busy-wait), configuring the GPS to emit only the RMC sentence (the default 8 sentences keep the UART busy about half of every second), and register-level drivers.

Race to idle

Running slower saves little because the core is already idle more than 99.9 % of the time; the current floor is the peripherals moving data and the Stop 1 floor.

2. Computation

The unmodified firmware sources were built with a class that counts every floating-point add, multiply, divide, compare and conversion and every libm call, on three hours of simulated sensor streams. The counting build produces output identical to the plain build (maximum difference 0.0). Counts are then multiplied by Cortex-M4F cycle costs.

StageRunsFP add / mulFP divlog10flogfexpffloorfCycles (nominal)
1 Hz sample taskevery second1530110546
Feature extractionevery 30 s2,0044614200037,444
int8 MLP 25-32-16-5every 30 s1395005257,913

142 log10f calls per window dominate feature extraction: the same value is recomputed in several loops. The 1,392 int8 multiply-accumulates of the MLP are added at 3.5 cycles each (scalar C).

Optimisation ladder, each step checked against the reference firmware

VariantCycles / hopµsLabels identicalDifferent source answeredAnswer ↔ uncertain flipsMax prob. change
v0 Reference firmware80,861476100.00%000.000
v1 + log10 cached per second62,057365100.00%000.000
v2 + humidity term every 10 s56,95933599.72%010.419
v3 + polynomial log / exp47,53728099.72%010.419
v4 + SIMD int8 MLP (estimated)44,32226199.72%010.419

v1 is bit-identical. v2 and v3 change 1 of 357 windows, an answer flipping to or from “uncertain”, and no window changes from one source to another. The largest single-window probability change is 0.42, caused by the numerically fragile feature discussed below. v4 uses SMLAD / CMSIS-NN style int8 dot products, which give identical integers; its cycle count is an estimate until measured. A first attempt at the humidity step (hold one noisy reading for 10 s) was rejected by exactly this check: it moved the gas features enough to flip windows, so the final version averages ten readings before evaluating the exponential once.

A numerically fragile feature

Comparing windows after the humidity change showed that pm_gas_corr (the correlation between particle count and gas response, computed from about 12 points per window) swings by 0.3 to 0.4 for a 0.003 change in gas resistance. Removing it changes the MLP from 0.937 to 0.925 and the forest from 0.923 to 0.921; also removing skew and variation gives 0.919 and 0.914. It is not clearly harmful in the simulator, so no change is recommended, but features built from so few points deserve a second look on real, noisier data.

Where the computation story is, and is not

  • Is: a fixed-memory, no-malloc pipeline with bounded loops (3.4 KB of state) whose worst-case time is known; it fits a small Cortex-M4F with more than 99.9 % of the CPU idle; the architecture around it, not the arithmetic, sets the energy.
  • Is not: an energy claim for the algorithm itself. The whole inference costs 28 µJ per 30 s, about 0.9 µW averaged, against hundreds of milliwatts for the sensors.
  • Headroom: at 1 % CPU duty the budget is 51 M cycles per hop, about 631x the current pipeline. That room could hold an ensemble, on-device uncertainty estimates, a longer feature window, online baseline adaptation or self-calibration, which are the places to look for a computation contribution.

A burst is 90 s (30 s fan warm-up plus a full 60 s window). “Answer shown is right” counts the last answer held for up to 10 minutes, which is what a user sees; counting only fresh answers would unfairly penalise duty cycling. The gas-triggered policy (wake the PMS7003 when the BME688 signal departs from its recent median; threshold 0.1 chosen on separate development days) fails because only 24% of source windows trip it. Dust and some combustion sources barely move the gas sensor.

4. What the device is verified against

Three different things are verified, and each needs a different reference: how much particulate there is (mass and size), which gases are present, and which source it came from. The third has no instrument that simply reads it out, so it is verified in layers, from strongest to weakest evidence.

QuantityReferenceResolution and how it is usedWhere to get it
PM2.5 massFEM / regulatory monitor (beta-attenuation, TEOM, or an optical monitor with FEM status) at an official air-quality station; filter-based gravimetric sampling is the gold standardHourly or 24 h. Co-locate at least 3 units for at least 30 days. EPA PM2.5 sensor targets apply (below).Station co-location through the state pollution control board or a university partner
Particle size binsReference optical particle sizer or aerodynamic particle sizer (APS-class) in a chamber; a second reference OPC outdoorsVerifies the six PMS7003 bins and the coarse-particle under-response the model assumes.University aerosol lab

Only the PM2.5 targets come from an external protocol, and they apply to mass, not to source labels. The others are proposals to agree with your supervisor before collecting data.

Pitfalls that ruin a verification

  • Time alignment. Log in UTC everywhere. A one-hour offset or averaging periods that start on different minutes costs more R² than any sensor error.
  • Reference conditions. FEM monitors report dry mass after conditioning; the PMS7003 does not dry its sample. Record RH on both.
  • Split by day and by site, never by window. Neighbouring windows are almost identical, so a random split inflates accuracy.
  • Freeze the model before the blind phase and write down its file hash, thresholds and firmware version.
  • Label noise sets a ceiling. An observer who is wrong 10 % of the time makes a perfect device look worse; report the gap (the rehearsal shows it below).
  • Intervals need independent samples. Windows within one episode are not independent; plan in episodes and days.
  • Log raw data (counts and per-step gas resistance at 1 Hz) so the labels can be recomputed with a better model.

Closing the loop between simulation and reality

After the first week of real data run python -m verify.domain_gap sim.csv real.csv. It trains a classifier to tell simulated windows from real ones: an area under the curve of 0.5 means indistinguishable and 1.0 means the simulator is far off. It also ranks the 25 features by how much they differ and names the group of parameters in params.py to fix first. Re-fit, re-run run_all.py, and track that one number down.

5. Rehearsal on simulated data

Three prototypes next to a simulated FEM-class monitor, reference gas analysers, tracer chemistry and an observer log for 12 days of 8 h; corrections are scored by 4-fold cross-validation over whole days, so every hour is predicted by a correction that never saw its own day. Each reference carries its own error, so the analysis is exercised against imperfect references. The file formats it reads and writes are in results/verification/.

Particle mass

Every hour predicted by a correction fitted on other days. Left to right: raw device reading, humidity correction, and a correction in which the device's own source attribution selects the gain.

Why the raw reading is hard to correct in the simulator: the same sensor reads different sources differently (small combustion particles are under-counted, hygroscopic ones over-counted). The size of this effect is an assumption of the simulator, so its size on real hardware is the thing to measure.

Source attribution

For context: on the six 24-hour strong-source field days of the main campaign the same device answers correctly 97% of the time when it answers (at 78% coverage). The rehearsal places sources at random distances and bearings, so many episodes are faint or short, and its observer labels carry about 10 % error; both lower the score, which is what a real, messy campaign will also do.

Rows are the observer's label, columns the device's. Macro-F1 0.58 (95 % interval 0.43-0.61) against the observer; 0.67 against the hidden truth. The gap is the cost of an imperfect reference.

Blocks are counted over three units that see the same air, so independent episodes are far fewer (last column; many are short fragments where a faint plume crosses the 40 % dominance threshold). Per-class values from a dozen days are therefore very noisy: biomass burning has few, short episodes in this site mix and none were recognised, which a longer campaign would resolve. Co-located units agree on 100% of windows.

How much data is enough

Left: the 95 % interval on macro-F1 narrows as days are added (this site mix, resampled by day). Right: a recall near 0.90 is only pinned down to ±0.05 with roughly 140 independent episodes; with 30 it is ±0.11. Plan the number of episodes per class, not hours.

What this work changed in the simulator

  • PMS7003 sample heating added. Rehearsing the PM2.5 comparison showed device readings of thousands of µg/m³ in near-fog air, because particles grew with the ambient humidity. A real PMS7003 warms the sample by a few degrees inside its housing (assumed +5 °C here) and field comparisons show 2-3x over-reading at high humidity, not 70x. The effective humidity is now lower and capped at 95 %. The 16-test campaign was re-run: 11 of 16 tests meet their criteria now, 9 of 16 before. The earlier run is kept in results/previous_run/.
  • Firmware variants (FW_OPT_* flags in polso_fw.c) are off by default; the reference build is unchanged apart from profiling hooks.
  • Humidity decimation was first written as “hold one reading for 10 s”; the equivalence check rejected it and it now averages ten readings.
  • Correction of an earlier note: params.py described a “Stop 2” low-power mode. The G4 family has Stop 0 and Stop 1 only.

UART overrunsCount lost bytes on the GPS and PMS ports over 24 hRing-buffer risk
Stop 1 wake time, PMS frame period, BME688 read timeLogic analyser on a GPIO / SCLWake penalty and schedule assumptions

Still to confirm from the ST datasheet (DS12288, not retrievable when this was written): run-mode current at 170 MHz, Stop 1 current, flash wait states at 170 MHz in boost mode, and whether DMA can reach the CCM SRAM. The G4 family has Sleep, Stop 0, Stop 1, Standby and Shutdown; it has no “Stop 2”.

Reproduce

cd environment_simulation
python run_all.py          # train + the 16-test campaign          (~12 min)
python run_mcu.py          # STM32 twin                              (~15 min)
python run_verification.py # virtual co-location rehearsal            (~2 min)
python build_report.py     # this report
python -m unittest discover tests

Total run time of the STM32 twin: 8 min; verification rehearsal: 1.0 min.
